etymologies.heading: Etymology
paragraphs: First attested in 1526, from Middle English abrogat (“abolished”), from Latin abrogātus, perfect passive participle of abrogō (“repeal”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + rogō (“ask, inquire, propose”). See rogation.
senses: (transitive, law) To annul (as a law, decree, ordinance, etc.) by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or their successor; to repeal.[First attested in the early 16th century.]
(transitive) To put an end to; to do away with. [First attested in the early 16th century.]
(archaic) Abrogated; abolished. [First attested from around (1350 to 1470).]
